A teddy bear has a rounded head, short protruding muzzle, two small ears high on the head, and a soft torso with four stubby limbs. Its plush fabric may be beige, brown, cream, or another colour, with a visible pile that changes shade when brushed against its grain. The nose is usually stitched or molded; eyes are small dark buttons or securely fixed plastic, depending on the toy. Seams follow the sides of the limbs and body. It slumps when set down, compresses in someone’s arms, and springs back imperfectly. Handling makes a faint fabric rustle, not a mechanical sound.

Inflated latex balloons are smooth, thin-skinned ovals with a narrower neck tied into a small knot. Their colours look saturated in shade and translucent where strong light passes through; a window or ceiling lamp appears as a bright reflection on the curved surface. Air-filled balloons fall slowly, bounce lightly, and roll along the floor. Helium-filled ones pull upward against a narrow curling ribbon, bobbing with drafts or a person’s movement. They squeak when rubbed together and make a light tapping sound against a wall. Party clusters vary slightly in size and shape, even when the colours match.

A wedding cake is commonly presented on a rigid round board or stand, often with two or more round tiers that narrow upward. Smooth buttercream or fondant may cover the sides in white or pale colours, with piped borders, sugar flowers, or fresh flowers placed deliberately along the tiers. The tiers are level but handmade decoration has tiny irregularities; fresh petals cast small shadows. Its height reaches roughly from a person’s waist toward their chest when displayed on a table. A knife meets slight resistance through icing, then softer sponge. Serving produces quiet plate and cutlery clinks amid conversation.

A birthday cake is usually a low round or rectangular sponge cake on a cardboard cake board, covered with buttercream, whipped cream, or glossy icing. Piped edges, coloured sprinkles, fruit, or chocolate pieces sit on top; lettering, if present, follows the cake’s curve and is rarely perfectly uniform. Thin candles stand in the icing, their small flames bending with nearby movement and reflecting on glossy decorations. A person can carry the cake with both hands. Plates and forks clink as it is served, candles make a faint hiss when blown out, and a knife leaves cream on each cut face.

A chocolate box is a shallow, rigid cardboard box, commonly rectangular or square, with a fitted lid. Printed branding belongs on the actual package, not as a floating label; an unbranded box can have a plain coloured lid. Inside, small chocolates sit in individual cavities of a molded plastic tray or pleated paper cups, sometimes beneath a thin protective sheet. Their surfaces range from matte cocoa dust to glossy tempered chocolate, with slight differences in shape and decoration. The lid lifts without hinges and may rub softly against the base. The tray crackles when handled; chocolates make muted taps as they are picked up.

topic: Iraqi tea set on a tray
body: An Iraqi tea service sits on a round metal tray with a shallow raised rim, often stainless steel or engraved brass-coloured metal. Small, clear, handleless istikan glasses have narrow waists and flared lips; each stands on a little saucer. Strong black tea fills the lower part of each glass in a deep reddish amber, leaving room near the rim. A small teapot and sugar bowl may share the tray, with teaspoons resting on saucers. Someone carries the tray level with one hand beneath it or both hands at its edges. Glass and spoon make delicate clinks; poured tea sounds like a thin, steady splash.

A whole watermelon is a heavy oval or round fruit, commonly about the width of a person’s torso, with a smooth, firm rind. Its green skin shows irregular darker green stripes or mottling and a duller patch where it rested on the ground. Cut open, it reveals thick pale rind around red or pink flesh, often dotted with flat dark seeds, though some varieties have only small pale seed traces. The cut surface looks wet and glistens in sunlight. A knife passes through the flesh easily but needs more pressure at the rind. Slices drip juice, thud softly on a plate, and crunch wetly when bitten.

A pomegranate is a round, slightly flattened fruit about the size of a fist, with tough, leathery skin ranging from warm yellow-red to deep crimson. A small, stiff, star-shaped crown protrudes from one end. The skin is matte to faintly glossy and may show natural scuffs or fine cracks. Cutting it reveals pale, spongy membranes separating tightly packed, translucent red or pink arils, each enclosing a seed. A ripe fruit feels heavy. Arils tumble and bounce when loosened into a bowl, making soft taps; biting them gives a crisp pop. In Iraqi markets, whole fruits sit in shallow crates or are split to display their colour.

Oranges are roughly spherical citrus fruits, usually palm-sized, with a dimpled peel coloured bright orange to yellow-orange. Their skins vary in thickness and often show a small green stem scar; some retain a leaf. Beneath the peel is white, fibrous pith around wedge-shaped segments filled with juice sacs. A knife makes a soft rasp through the rind, while peeling releases tiny sprays of aromatic oil. Segments separate with a faint tear and release juice when squeezed. In a fruit stall, oranges pile unevenly in crates rather than forming perfect rows, with natural variation in size, colour and surface marks.

Bananas grow in connected hands, each fruit attached by a short, thick stalk. An individual banana is elongated and gently curved, with several subtle lengthwise ridges and a tapered tip. Market bananas are commonly green-yellow, clear yellow or yellow with scattered brown ripening freckles; the peel may have small pressure bruises. Inside, the flesh is pale cream and soft but holds its shape when freshly peeled. Pulling a peel strip downward makes a faint fibrous rip, and slicing gives a muted tap on a board. Hands of bananas hang from stall hooks or rest in crates, shifting slightly when lifted by their shared stem.

Grapes hang in branching clusters from a thin central stem, with individual berries attached on finer stalks. Berries may be small and round or slightly oval, coloured pale green, amber, red or dark purple depending on the variety. Fresh skins can carry a dusty-looking natural wax bloom, not dirt. A cluster bends under its own weight, and loose berries roll quickly across a table. Pulling one free makes a tiny snap; biting it breaks the taut skin with a soft pop and releases clear juice. At produce stalls, clusters lie in shallow crates, their slender stems visible between the fruit.

Tomatoes and cucumbers are commonly displayed together at Iraqi vegetable stalls and chopped together for salad. Tomatoes are rounded or slightly flattened, with smooth red skin, a small stem scar and moist chambers of seeds inside; some still carry a green, star-shaped calyx. Cucumbers are elongated, firm and dark to medium green, often with faint lengthwise stripes and a subtly bumpy surface. A knife meets tomato skin with slight resistance before releasing juice; cucumber cuts with a sharper, watery crunch. Chopped pieces glisten in a bowl, while whole vegetables roll or shift naturally when picked up from a crate.

Iraqi torshi is a mixture of vegetables preserved in a sharp brine or vinegar liquid, often served beside rice, sandwiches or grilled food. A clear jar or bowl may show cauliflower florets, carrot rounds, cucumber pieces, turnip and peppers packed irregularly together. Colours range from pale cream and orange to green; turnip can appear vivid pink when pickled with beet. The vegetables stay firm enough to crunch rather than collapsing. Liquid clings to each piece and drips back into the jar when lifted with a spoon. Glass clinks softly against the spoon, followed by a wet stir and a crisp bite.

Iraqi amba is a tangy mango pickle or sauce, typically mustard-yellow to deep golden, with a thick, uneven texture rather than the smooth look of bottled juice. Small softened mango pieces may be visible in the spiced liquid. In a jar it coats the glass above the fill line; on a sandwich or plate it spreads in glossy streaks and slowly settles into folds. A spoon lifts it in a heavy ribbon that drops with a soft plop. Amba is commonly added to Iraqi falafel sandwiches and other street food, where its bright colour contrasts with bread, vegetables and browned fried fillings.

Iraqi geymar is a thick, pale ivory dairy cream served at breakfast, often in a shallow dish with dark date syrup poured over or beside it. The cream sits in soft folds or broad scoops, with a delicate wrinkled surface skin and edges that hold their shape. Date syrup is translucent deep brown where thin and nearly black where it pools; it runs slowly into glossy ribbons over the cream. A spoon presses through the dense, yielding geymar with little sound, then lightly taps the dish. Torn samoon or other bread is used to scoop up both, leaving irregular swirls of cream and syrup.

Iraqi lentil soup is a smooth, opaque golden-yellow to orange soup, usually made from red lentils cooked until they lose their shape. It fills a small ceramic bowl nearly to the rim and may have tiny flecks of cumin or black pepper on its surface. It pours in a thick, continuous stream rather than splashing like water. A spoon leaves a shallow trail that slowly closes. Serve it hot with a lemon wedge and flatbread; a squeeze of lemon makes small ripples across the surface. Steam rises in soft wisps under side light. The scene is quiet except for spoon taps against the bowl and bread tearing.

Iraqi biryani is a piled platter of separate long rice grains, predominantly yellow from spices, with some white and deeper orange patches. Chicken pieces or cooked meat sit among small cubes of fried potato, peas, carrots and short browned strands of vermicelli. Raisins and toasted nuts may be scattered over the top; some servings include halved boiled eggs. It is mixed rather than built as perfectly defined layers. A serving spoon lifts loose grains and heavier pieces together, with a few raisins rolling back onto the platter. The rice gives off light steam when fresh. Plates, spoons and small side dishes sit around a family table.

Tepsi baytinjan fills a shallow round or rectangular metal baking tray. Fried eggplant slices show dark purple skin around soft brown centres, overlapping with pale golden potato slices, red tomato rounds and onion. Depending on the household, small meatballs or seasoned minced meat sit between the vegetables. A red tomato sauce pools in the gaps and stains the tray edges; the top has browned spots from the oven, not a thick cheese crust. When a spoon cuts in, tender slices slide apart and sauce runs into the space. The tray may arrive bubbling faintly, then settle with a soft sizzle. Serve beside white rice or bread.

Iraqi fasolia with rice is commonly presented as two distinct parts: a bowl of white beans in red tomato stew beside a mound of steamed white rice. The beans remain whole and plump, with glossy skins; small pieces of lamb or beef may be visible in the sauce. The stew is fluid enough to ladle but thick enough to coat the beans. Iraqi rice has visible separate grains and may have a lightly browned crisp portion from the bottom of the pot. A ladleful of fasolia spreads across the rice and sinks between grains. Gentle steam rises, accompanied by the clink of a ladle and plates.

Makhlama is served hot in a small frying pan or shallow plate, with eggs set among softened chopped tomatoes and onions. The tomatoes make a red, slightly oily sauce with visible skins and irregular pieces, rather than a smooth purée. Egg whites turn opaque while yolks may remain rounded and soft; in other servings, the eggs are stirred into yellow-and-red curds. Some versions contain browned minced meat, but the egg-and-tomato base stays visible. A metal spoon breaks a yolk and draws yellow across the sauce. The pan gives a brief hiss as it leaves the heat. Iraqi bread is used to scoop it up.

A shawarma spit is a tall vertical steel skewer carrying a dense stack of thin meat slices, shaped into a tapered cylinder roughly as high as a worker’s torso. The skewer stands over a circular drip tray, with upright gas burners or electric heating panels behind it. A motor turns the meat slowly and steadily, bringing every side past the heat; the outer layer darkens and glistens while the centre stays covered. A cook shaves thin strips downward with a long knife or electric cutter, and the pieces fall into the tray. There is a low motor hum, burner hiss and crisp scraping sound. Warm shop lights catch the rendered fat.

An Iraqi falafel sandwich often uses a small, elongated samoon loaf with a pointed end and a slit along one side. Several deep-fried falafel pieces sit inside, their rough brown crusts contrasting with a soft greenish interior where one is broken. Chopped tomato, cucumber, parsley and pickles may fill the gaps, with tahini sauce or tangy amba visible near the opening. The bread compresses slightly when held, and loose crumbs or salad pieces can fall onto the paper wrapper. A bite makes a brief crisp crunch followed by the softer sound of bread tearing. It is commonly assembled at a street-food counter.

Scooped ice cream forms rounded mounds with curved ridges left by the scoop. Its surface is matte and faintly grainy when very cold, becoming smoother and glossier as it warms. Vanilla is pale cream, chocolate is brown, and fruit flavours vary in colour; avoid making every flavour unnaturally bright. A scoop sits in a wafer cone or paper cup, visibly smaller than a person’s palm. In warm air, the edges soften first, then slow drips run down the cone or cup. A metal scoop scrapes against the tub, while a wafer cone gives a dry crunch when bitten. Shop display lights reflect on the glass freezer.

A small Iraqi juice shop has a bright Arabic sign above a glass-front counter, with oranges, lemons, pomegranates, and bananas displayed in crates or neat piles. Behind the counter sit a citrus press, blender, plastic pitchers, and rows of clear cups. A worker cuts fruit, presses halves under a metal cone, or runs a blender that buzzes sharply before stopping. Juice pours in a thick, uneven stream; pulp and foam gather at the top. Customers stand close to the counter while cups are filled, lidded, and handed over. Daylight catches condensation on cold pitchers and the wet shine of freshly cut fruit.

A common single-serve Pepsi bottle is clear molded PET plastic, roughly hand-height, with rounded shoulders, a narrow threaded neck, and a five-lobed base that lets it stand upright. Dark brown cola shows through the plastic. A blue wraparound label sits around the middle, carrying the red, white, and blue Pepsi globe and white Pepsi lettering; a blue screw cap seals the neck above a tamper-evident ring. Bottle sizes and label layouts vary by market. When lifted, the thin plastic flexes slightly. Opening the cap makes a short crackle and hiss; pouring produces fizz, rising bubbles, and a brief foam head.

A typical disposable drinking-water bottle is transparent PET plastic, narrow enough to hold in one hand, with a short threaded neck, a screw cap, and a tamper-evident ring left behind when first opened. Its sides often have shallow ribs or molded grip panels; the bottom has raised feet. A paper or plastic label wraps around the center, while the clear water reveals any dents in the bottle wall. The lightweight bottle crinkles when squeezed and springs partly back. Removing the cap makes a small plastic snap. Water glugs from the opening when tilted steeply and leaves clear beads of condensation if chilled.

A takeaway coffee cup is a tall, gently tapered paperboard cylinder, wider at its rolled rim than at its flat base. The inside has a thin liquid-resistant lining. A fitted plastic lid snaps over the rim, usually with a raised drinking spout or small sip opening; some cups have a separate corrugated cardboard sleeve around the middle. Branding, when present, is printed on the outside rather than inside the cup. An adult holds it comfortably in one hand, often by the sleeve. Hot coffee gives off faint steam through the opening. The lid clicks when pressed into place, and the cup makes a soft papery sound when set down.

A cappuccino with latte art sits in a small, wide ceramic cup, often on a matching saucer with a teaspoon beside it. Espresso gives the surface a warm brown edge; finely steamed milk forms a glossy, creamy layer with no large visible bubbles. A white heart or leaf pattern spreads across the brown surface, its curved edges made by the milk pour rather than a printed stencil. The cup is filled close to, but below, the rim. Freshly made, it releases a little steam. The pattern slowly blurs as the cup moves, and the saucer gives a light ceramic clink when lifted or set down.

An Arabic sweets tray is a broad, shallow metal serving tray holding small pastries in orderly rows or clusters. It may mix diamond-cut baklava, rolled pastries, round semolina pieces, and pistachio-topped bites; the exact assortment varies by shop. Golden pastry layers have crisp edges, while syrup gives their surfaces a restrained shine. Chopped green pistachio, pale nuts, and occasional paper cups separate pieces visually. A vendor lifts individual sweets with small tongs onto a plate or into a box. The tongs click against the tray, and flaky pieces make a faint crackle. Display-case lighting reflects off the metal rim and glossy syrup.

Kunafa is commonly presented as a shallow round pastry cooked in a wide metal pan and cut into wedges or squares. One familiar version has a crisp, finely shredded pastry surface, toasted from gold to orange-gold, over a soft white cheese filling. Another uses a finer, compact semolina-like crust. Clear sugar syrup adds a glossy sheen, and crushed green pistachios may be scattered across the top. A server slides a flat spatula beneath a portion; crisp strands shift and crackle while the warm filling can stretch in soft threads as the piece lifts. On a plate, a cut edge shows the thin crust above the thicker filling.

Basbousa is a shallow semolina cake baked in a rectangular or round pan and marked into small squares or diamonds. Its surface is evenly golden brown, slightly grainy rather than smooth, with a whole almond or pistachio sometimes pressed into the center of each portion. Sugar syrup soaks into the cake, leaving a moist sheen without hiding the scored lines. A spatula lifts one piece, exposing a dense, tender crumb made of visible fine grains. It holds its shape but releases a few crumbs at the cut edges. A knife makes a soft scraping sound against the pan, followed by the gentle tap of cake placed on a plate.
